'''''Eucalyptus tereticornis''''', commonly known as '''forest red gum''', '''blue gum''' or '''red irongum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''tereticornis'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_tereticornis_subsp._tereticornis.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref> is a species of tree that is native to eastern Australia and southern New Guinea. It has smooth bark, lance-shaped to curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven, nine or eleven, white flowers and hemispherical fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|20-50|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. The trunk is straight, usually unbranched for more than half of the total height of the tree and has a girth of up to {{cvt|2|m}} [[diameter at breast height|dbh]]. Thereafter, limbs are unusually steeply inclined for a ''Eucalyptus'' species. The bark is shed in irregular sheets, resulting in a smooth trunk surface coloured in patches of white, grey and blue, corresponding to areas that shed their bark at different times. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have dull bluish green, egg-shaped leaves that are {{cvt|60-130|mm}} long and {{cvt|30-80|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are the same shade of green on both sides, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|80-220|mm}} long and {{cvt|10-35|mm}} wide, tapering at the base to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|13-30|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of seven, nine or eleven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|7-25|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|2-6|mm}} long. Mature buds are an elongated oval shape, {{cvt|9-16|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-6|mm}} wide with a conical to horn-shaped [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] that is much longer than the [[Hypanthium|floral cup]]. Flowering has been recorded in most months and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, hemispherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|2-6|mm}} long and {{cvt|4-8|mm}} wide with the valves prominently protruding.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="Boland 1984">{{cite book | author = Boland, D. J. | year = 1984 | title = Forest Trees of Australia | edition = 4th | isbn = 0-643-05423-5|display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~tereticornis |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=7 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20tereticornis |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=7 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Messina |first1=Andre |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''mediana'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/1da6a400-fc28-4b10-8353-2d21ed6a5f12 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=7 January 2020}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' was first formally described 1795 by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in ''[[A Specimen of the Botany of New Holland]]'' from specimens collected in 1793 from [[Port Jackson]] by [[First Fleet]] surgeon and naturalist [[John White (surgeon)|John White]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454410|publisher=APNI|access-date=8 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="Sm.">{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=James Edward |title=A Specimen of the Botany of New Holland |date=1795 |publisher=James Sowerby |location=London |pages=[https://archive.org/details/zoologybotanyofn00shaw/page/41 41]–42 |access-date=8 January 2020|url=https://archive.org/details/zoologybotanyofn00shaw}}</ref><ref name="Boland 1984"/>  (Smith's volume was the botanical part of ''Zoology and Botany of New Holland''. The zoological part was written by [[George Shaw (biologist)|George Shaw]].) The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''tereticornis'') is from the [[Latin]] words ''teres'' (becoming ''tereti-'' in the combined form) meaning "[[wikt:terete|terete]]" and ''cornu'' meaning "horn", in reference to the horn-shaped operculum.<ref name="Boland">{{cite book |last1=Boland |first1=Douglas J. |last2=Brooker |first2=M. Ian H. |last3=Chippendale |first3=George M. |last4=Hall |first4=Norman |last5=Hyland |first5=Bernard P.M. |last6=Johnston |first6=Robert D. |last7=Kleinig |first7=David A. |last8=McDonald |first8=Maurice W. |last9=Turner |first9=John D. |title=Forest trees of Australia |url=https://archive.org/details/foresttreesaustr00bola |url-access=limited |date=2006 |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |location=Collingwood, Victoria |isbn=0-643-06969-0 |page=[https://archive.org/details/foresttreesaustr00bola/page/n354 322] |edition=5th.}}</ref>

In 1999 [[Ian Brooker]] and [[Andrew Slee]] described two subspecies and in 2013 [[Anthony Bean]] described a further two, and the names of these four subspecies are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:
* ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''basaltica'' <small>A.R.Bean</small><ref name="APC1">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''basaltica'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/246794|website=Australian Plant Census |access-date=8 January 2020}}</ref> has opercula that are not expanded at the base, juvenile leaves that are dull bluish, egg-shaped to round, up to one to two times as long as broad, and pedicels {{cvt|2.5-6|mm}} long;
* ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''mediana'' <small>Brooker & Slee</small><ref name="APC2">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''mediana'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/119639|website=Australian Plant Census |access-date=8 January 2020}}</ref> has opercula that are not expanded at the base, juvenile leaves that are dull bluish, egg-shaped to round, up to one to two times as long as broad, and pedicels {{cvt|1-3|mm}} long;
* ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''rotunda'' <small>A.R.Bean</small><ref name="APC3">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''rotunda''  |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/246797|website=Australian Plant Census |access-date=8 January 2020}}</ref> has opercula that are not expanded at the base, juvenile leaves that are green, round and up to 1.2 times as long as broad;
* ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' <small>Sm.</small> subsp. ''tereticornis''<ref name="APC4">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' subsp. ''tereticornis'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/153669|website=Australian Plant Census |access-date=8 January 2020}}</ref> has opercula expanded at the base and juvenile leaves that are lance-shaped to egg-shaped, and two to three times longer than wide.<ref name="A.R.Bean">{{cite journal |last1=Bean |first1=Anthony R. |title=Two new subspecies of ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' |journal=Austrobaileya |date=2013 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=107–112}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species has a wide distribution, occurring over the widest range of [[latitude]]s of any ''Eucalyptus'' species, occurring from southern [[Papua New Guinea]] at latitude [[15th parallel south|15°S]], to southeastern [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] at latitude [[38th parallel south|38°S]].<ref name="Boland"/> The forest red gum is one of the key [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] species of the threatened [[Cumberland Plain#Ecology|Cumberland Plain Woodlands]].<ref name="OEH">{{cite web|title=Cumberland Plain Woodland in the Sydney Basin Bioregion - profile|url=https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/threatenedSpeciesApp/profile.aspx?id=10191|access-date=8 September 2011|publisher=New South Wales Government Office of Environment and Heritage}}</ref>

Subspecies ''basaltica'' grows in eucalypt woodland from [[Kroombit Tops National Park|Kroombit Tops]] to near Sydney with a [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct]] population in the [[Carnarvon Range]]. Subspecies ''mediana'' is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern Victoria where it grows near river banks, wetlands, low hills and plains. Subspecies ''rotunda'' is endemic to a small area near [[Mitchell, Queensland|Mitchell]] in Queensland, growing along creek banks. Subspecies ''tereticornis'' is the most widely distributed of the four subspecies and grows in open forest from the [[Cape York Peninsula]] in Queensland, to near [[Bega, New South Wales|Bega]] in southern New South Wales and as far inland as [[Roma, Queensland|Roma]]. It is also known from the [[Central Province (Papua New Guinea)|Central]] and [[Oro Province]]s in Papua New Guinea.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="A.R.Bean" />

==Uses==
The tree has a strong, hard and durable heartwood, with a density of about 1100 kg m<sup>−3</sup>. It is used for construction in heavy engineering, such as for railway sleepers.<ref name="Boland"/> The leaves of ''E. tereticornis'' are used in the production of [[cineole]] based [[eucalyptus oil]].<ref>Boland, D.J., Brophy, J.J., and A.P.N. House, ''Eucalyptus Leaf Oils'', 1991, {{ISBN|0-909605-69-6}}</ref>

==Regional ecosystems==
Some regional ecosystems in [[Queensland, Australia|Queensland]] which contain ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' as a dominant or co-dominant tree species are classified as 'of concern' or 'endangered' under the Queensland [[Vegetation Management Act 1999]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Vegetation management regional ecosystem description - ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' (endangered) |url=https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/land/management/vegetation/maps/regional-ecosystem-list?redesc=eucalyptus+tereticornis&revmac=Endangered&rebds= |website=Queensland Government |publisher=Queensland Government |access-date=13 November 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Vegetation management regional ecosystem description - ''Eucalyptus tereticornis'' (Of Concern) |url=https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/land/management/vegetation/maps/regional-ecosystem-list?redesc=eucalyptus+tereticornis&revmac=Of+concern&rebds= |website=Queensland Government |publisher=Queensland Government |access-date=13 November 2025}}</ref> Forest and woodlands of this species which occur on alluvium  have been extensively cleared for agriculture. Remnant vegetation in the South-East Queensland Bioregion are listed as endangered with less than 10% of their preclearing extent remaining.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hogan |first1=Luke |last2=Smith |first2=Geoffrey |title=The birds of remnant forest red gum (''Eucalyptus tereticornis'') forest |journal=Sunbird |date=2013 |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=29-44 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/314115317_The_birds_of_remnant_forest_red_gum_Eucalyptus_tereticornis_forest}}</ref>
